common_name: Variegata Cornelian Cherry (White-Margined Variegated Cornus mas)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in full sun to part shade on well-drained soil; a second seedling or cultivar nearby improves fruit set, and afternoon shade in hot climates helps prevent leaf scorch on the white margins.

directions: Variegata is a slower-growing, more compact sport of cornelian cherry grown chiefly as a foliage specimen, with leaves broadly edged in creamy white that brighten shaded corners of the garden through the growing season. Like the species it opens tiny yellow flowers on bare stems in late winter, well ahead of the foliage, and can still set the typical tart red, cherry-like drupes if a compatible pollinator is nearby, though fruiting is generally lighter than on green-leaved cultivars. Because variegated foliage is more prone to scorch, site it out of hot afternoon sun in warmer zones. Otherwise it shares the species' tolerance for a wide range of soils, drought once established, and urban conditions, and its slower, denser habit suits it well to smaller gardens.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Cornus mas

common_name: Aurea Golden-Leaved Cornelian Cherry (Yellow-Foliage Cornus mas Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in early spring in full sun to light part shade; give Aurea some protection from harsh midday sun in hot climates, since intense heat can scorch or bleach the yellow foliage to a washed-out green.

directions: Aurea is an older golden-leaved sport of cornelian cherry, opening chartreuse-yellow new growth each spring that softens toward yellow-green as summer heat advances, giving the shrub a bright, sunlit presence long after its late-winter yellow flower display has faded. It sets the species' typical tart, cherry-like red drupes when a compatible pollinator is nearby, and shares the same excellent cold hardiness, drought tolerance once established, and adaptability to a wide range of soils and urban sites. Foliage color is strongest with morning sun and some afternoon relief in warmer zones; deep shade will cause the leaves to revert toward plain green. Use it as a season-long color accent or informal screen where a golden-foliage large shrub is wanted.
sources: Dirr's Manual of Woody Landscape Plants

common_name: Elegantissima Tricolor Cornelian Cherry (Pink-and-White Variegated Cornus mas)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in part shade to full morning sun; the tricolor foliage of Elegantissima is prone to scorch in hot, exposed sites, so afternoon shade is especially important in zone 7-8 gardens.

directions: Elegantissima, also sold as Aureoelegantissima, is the showiest of the variegated cornelian cherry cultivars, with leaves splashed yellow and cream and flushed pink to rose along the margins, an effect that intensifies in cooler spring and fall weather. It flowers on bare branches in late winter like the species and can produce the typical tart red drupes when cross-pollinated, though it is grown primarily as a specimen foliage shrub rather than for fruit. Because strong variegation reduces overall vigor, growth is slower and more compact than green-leaved cornelian cherry, and plants benefit from some shelter from harsh afternoon sun and wind to keep leaf color from scorching. Otherwise it is as cold-hardy and adaptable as the species, tolerating a range of soils once established.
sources: De Nolf Plant Guide — Cornus mas 'Aurea Elegantissima'

common_name: Vydubetsky Cornelian Cherry (Red Star, Ukrainian Long-Fruited Cornus mas Selection)

planting.note: Plant a grafted or rooted-cutting tree in early spring while dormant, in full sun on well-drained soil; a genetically distinct cornelian cherry planted nearby improves the already heavy fruit set typical of this cultivar.

directions: Vydubetsky, sometimes marketed as Red Star, is a Ukrainian cornelian cherry cultivar released in 1990 by breeder Svitlana Klymenko at the M.M. Hryshko National Botanical Garden in Kyiv, selected for its unusually long, elongated dark-red fruit that can reach over an inch in length. It is one of the most productive named Cornus mas selections, with mature specimens reported to bear well over 100 pounds of fruit in a good year, and the flesh is tender yet firm with a sweet-tart, refreshing flavor suited to fresh eating once fully ripe as well as jams, syrups, and cordials. Like other cornelian cherries it opens small yellow flowers on bare branches in late winter, is extremely cold-hardy, and tolerates drought, alkaline soils, and urban pollution once established. Harvest when fruit is deep red and slightly soft for the best flavor.
sources: M.M. Hryshko National Botanical Garden, National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine — Cornus mas breeding program (S. Klymenko)

common_name: Yantarnyi Cornelian Cherry (Amber, Ukrainian Yellow-Fruited Cornus mas Selection)

planting.note: Plant a grafted or rooted-cutting tree in early spring while dormant, in full sun on well-drained soil; pair with a red-fruited cornelian cherry cultivar nearby to ensure reliable cross-pollination and heavy fruit set.

directions: Yantarnyi, meaning "amber" and sometimes sold under that translated name, is a Ukrainian cornelian cherry cultivar introduced in 1982 by breeder Svitlana Klymenko at the M.M. Hryshko National Botanical Garden in Kyiv. It bears an abundant crop of oval, translucent amber-yellow fruit around an inch long, with a more delicate, fragrant, and less astringent flavor than red-fruited seedlings, making it especially pleasant eaten fresh in addition to preserves, syrups, and light-colored cornelian cherry jelly. Like the species it flowers on bare stems in late winter, is extremely cold-hardy, and tolerates drought, alkaline soils, and urban conditions once established. Its bright fruit color makes it a striking companion planting alongside red-fruited cultivars such as Vydubetsky or Pioneer.
sources: M.M. Hryshko National Botanical Garden, National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine — Cornus mas breeding program (S. Klymenko)
